htn_kidney.abstract: Approximately 5% of patients who develop renal rupture lack an identifiable underlying lesion, such as tumours, hydronephrosis, or vascular malformations. In this case report, we detail a case with a left renal rupture of a 29-year-old male diagnosed with IgA nephropathy (IgAN) and hypertensive nephropathy by renal biopsy. The patient was hospitalized with hypertension accompanied by renal dysfunction and heart failure. Before the onset of renal rupture, he had been initiated on corticosteroids for IgAN, and anticoagulant for persistent atrial fibrillation. portal_hypertension.abstract: There are 3 main pulmonary complications of cirrhosis-hepatic hydrothorax, hepatopulmonary syndrome, and portopulmonary hypertension-which are a result of portal hypertension. The presence of any of these complications should result in a referral to a liver transplant center as they portend an increase in mortality. In the United States, there are standard OPTN Model for End-Stage Liver Disease exception point guidelines and policies for these 3 pulmonary complications of cirrhosis that can assist in expediting transplant for these patient populations.

portal_hypertension.abstract: Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is a high-risk, often reversible cause of kidney failure in advanced cirrhosis. This review summarizes current concepts in epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, practical diagnosis of HRS, and management principles. We highlight the hemodynamic cascade of portal hypertension, splanchnic vasodilation, and neurohormonal activation, and the amplifying role of systemic inflammation. We provide a stepwise approach to evaluation, including albumin-guided volume assessment, accurate glomerular filtration rate estimation, and utilization of cystatin C and urinary biomarkers. portal_hypertension.abstract: Ascites and hyponatremia in cirrhosis both arise from portal hypertension-induced splanchnic vasodilation, leading to reduced effective arterial blood volume and neurohormonal activation. Ascites represents the most common decompensating event in cirrhosis and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality, while hyponatremia independently predicts poor prognosis and transplant outcomes. This article outlines evidence-based diagnostic strategies and stepwise management, including dietary modification, diuretics, paracentesis, transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt and transplant referral, as well as emerging therapies. portal_hypertension.abstract: Variceal bleeding is a life-threatening complication of portal hypertension, though mortality has been dramatically reduced by advances in acute management and prophylaxis. Management of acute variceal bleeding includes vasoactive drugs, antibiotics, restrictive transfusion, and endoscopic therapy within 12 hours. Endovascular techniques such as transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt and retrograde transvenous obliteration may be required in select or refractory cases. Prevention of variceal bleeding entails identifying at-risk patients with clinically significant portal hypertension and decreasing portal pressure with nonselective beta blockers (preferably carvedilol). portal_hypertension.abstract: Patients with cirrhosis are at increased risk of perioperative complications due to the systemic consequences of portal hypertension, altered hemostasis, ascites, malnutrition, sarcopenia, and immune dysfunction. These abnormalities predispose patients to bleeding, infection, impaired wound healing, and postoperative hepatic decompensation, even after otherwise routine surgical procedures. Active hepatic decompensations or even the presence of clinically significant portal hypertension alone substantially increase operative risk.
